sa-m04.title: Modeling Architecture Without Drowning in Detail

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 1-2. Supplemental: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 terminology. This unit focuses on what software architecture is for.

Software architecture is not just a diagram of major components. It is the set of significant design decisions that shape a system, the rationale behind those decisions, and the structures that allow stakeholders to reason about the system before every detail is implemented.

Rozanski and Woods frame architecture as a practical discipline for working with stakeholders. The architect must expose the important tradeoffs, make design choices visible, and keep the architecture connected to real concerns such as cost, risk, operability, performance, security, and delivery constraints.
Studio: choose a familiar software product and list five decisions that would be architectural rather than local implementation details. For each decision, identify who would care and why.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 1-2. Supplemental: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 terminology. This unit focuses on architecture description and architecture reality.

An architecture description is a communicative artifact. It may include views, diagrams, principles, models, decisions, scenarios, constraints, and explanations. The real architecture is the system and its consequential design choices; the description is the recorded representation used for communication and analysis.

This distinction matters because documentation can become either too vague to guide work or too exhaustive to maintain. Good architecture description records the structures and decisions that stakeholders need for design, review, implementation, testing, deployment, and evolution.
Studio: compare a code repository README, a deployment diagram, and a decision record. Decide which parts describe the architecture and which parts merely describe project logistics.

concepts.name: Documentation fitness

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 1-2. Supplemental: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 terminology. This unit focuses on qualities, constraints, and tradeoffs.

Architecture work becomes concrete when it connects structure to qualities. Performance, modifiability, security, availability, scalability, usability, deployability, and cost all create pressure on design. These qualities rarely improve together for free.
The architect therefore treats tradeoffs as first-class material. A design should make it possible to explain what quality was prioritized, which risks remain, and what evidence supports the choice.
Studio: describe one architectural decision as a tradeoff sentence: We chose X to improve Y, accepting risk Z under constraint C.

concepts.description: A situation where improving one architectural concern can weaken or complicate another concern.

modules.title: Week 2: Scope, Context, and System Boundaries

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 6-7 and 16. Supplemental: C4 system context guidance. This unit focuses on system context and environment.

Before designing internals, architects define the system boundary. A context view explains what the system is responsible for, which external people and systems it interacts with, and what assumptions exist at the boundary.
A clear context helps prevent scope drift and hidden integration risk. It also creates a shared language for business sponsors, users, developers, operators, security reviewers, and partner teams.
Studio: draw a system context diagram for an appointment scheduling platform. Include users, external systems, inbound flows, outbound flows, and trust boundaries.

concepts.name: System boundary
concepts.description: The line separating the system under design from users, external systems, and environmental dependencies.

concepts.name: System context
concepts.description: The external setting of a system, including actors, neighboring systems, interfaces, assumptions, and constraints.

concepts.name: External dependency
concepts.description: A person, organization, system, service, data source, or platform outside the system boundary that affects behavior.

concepts.name: Trust boundary
concepts.description: A boundary where data or control crosses between zones with different levels of trust or authority.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 6-7 and 16. Supplemental: C4 system context guidance. This unit focuses on architectural scope and responsibility.

Architecture scope determines which concerns the architecture must address. Scope can be product-level, system-level, subsystem-level, platform-level, or enterprise-level. Confusion about scope causes teams to over-design local details or under-design cross-cutting decisions.

Responsibility boundaries clarify ownership. A module, service, component, team, or external provider may own a decision. The architecture should make ownership clear enough that future changes have accountable paths.
Studio: classify five decisions from a current app as product, system, subsystem, or component-scope decisions.

concepts.name: Architecture scope
concepts.description: The span of system, organization, lifecycle, and decision-making concerns covered by an architecture effort.

concepts.name: Responsibility boundary
concepts.description: A boundary that clarifies which element, team, or party owns a capability or decision.

concepts.name: Ownership model
concepts.description: The assignment of responsibility for architectural elements, decisions, operations, and change.

concepts.name: Scope creep
concepts.description: Expansion of expected responsibility beyond the agreed system boundary or architecture goal.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 6-7 and 16. Supplemental: C4 system context guidance. This unit focuses on assumptions and environmental constraints.

Architectures are built under assumptions: expected user volume, network reliability, legal jurisdiction, existing platforms, team capabilities, budget, release cadence, and operational support. Hidden assumptions turn into defects when the environment changes.
Good architecture work records assumptions and tests the fragile ones. The point is not to predict everything, but to identify which assumptions would force redesign if they were false.
Studio: write six assumptions for a cloud-hosted learning platform, then mark the two most dangerous assumptions if wrong.

concepts.name: Architecture assumption
concepts.description: A belief about context, usage, technology, organization, or environment that influences architectural decisions.

concepts.name: Environmental constraint
concepts.description: A condition outside the system that restricts acceptable architecture choices.

concepts.name: Assumption validation
concepts.description: The process of checking whether important architecture assumptions are true enough to rely on.

concepts.name: Integration risk
concepts.description: Risk caused by uncertain behavior at interfaces with external systems, services, teams, or data sources.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 8-10. Supplemental: SEI architecture evaluation material. This unit focuses on identifying stakeholders.

Stakeholders include far more than end users and sponsors. Operators, testers, security teams, support staff, auditors, data owners, maintainers, developers, adjacent system teams, and future project teams may all rely on architectural choices.
Stakeholder analysis is not a formality. It is the mechanism that reveals concerns early enough to shape architecture rather than appear later as costly rework.
Studio: build a stakeholder map for an online banking feature and write one architectural concern for each stakeholder group.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 8-10. Supplemental: SEI architecture evaluation material. This unit focuses on scenarios as architectural test cases.

A scenario turns a vague quality into a testable architectural concern. Instead of saying the system must be fast, a scenario names the stimulus, source, environment, artifact, response, and response measure.
Scenarios are powerful because they connect stakeholders to evidence. They make architecture evaluation practical by asking what the system must do under specific conditions.
Studio: rewrite three vague requirements as quality attribute scenarios with measurable response criteria.

concepts.description: A structured statement that makes a quality concern testable through stimulus, environment, response, and response measure.

concepts.name: Stimulus
concepts.description: The event or condition that triggers a system response in a scenario.

concepts.name: Response measure
concepts.description: The observable criterion used to judge whether a scenario response is acceptable.

concepts.name: Scenario prioritization
concepts.description: The process of ranking scenarios by stakeholder importance, risk, cost, and architectural impact.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 8-10. Supplemental: SEI architecture evaluation material. This unit focuses on principles, constraints, and decisions.
Principles are durable design guidelines that help teams make consistent choices. They are useful only when they connect to real concerns and can be used to explain decisions.

A good decision record captures context, decision, status, consequences, and rationale. This lets future teams see why the architecture is the way it is, rather than reverse-engineering intent from code and diagrams.
Studio: write one architecture principle and one decision record for a system that must support offline mobile use.

concepts.description: A durable design guideline used to make related architectural decisions consistent and explainable.

concepts.name: Decision record
concepts.description: A concise record of an architectural choice, its context, rationale, status, and consequences.

concepts.name: Decision consequence
concepts.description: An expected effect, tradeoff, obligation, or risk introduced by an architecture decision.

concepts.name: Principle traceability
concepts.description: The ability to connect architectural decisions back to stated principles and stakeholder concerns.

modules.title: Week 4: Styles, Patterns, and Architectural Models

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 11-12. Supplemental: C4 model notation guidance. This unit focuses on architectural styles and patterns.

Architectural styles and patterns are reusable design forms. Layered architecture, pipes and filters, event-driven architecture, client-server, microservices, and shared data styles each make some qualities easier and others harder.
Patterns should not be selected because they are fashionable. A pattern is useful when its forces match the system context, stakeholder concerns, team capability, and expected evolution.
Studio: choose two styles for the same product idea and compare their effects on deployability, latency, modifiability, and operational complexity.

concepts.name: Architectural style
concepts.description: A named family of architectural organization with characteristic elements, relationships, and constraints.

concepts.name: Architectural pattern
concepts.description: A reusable solution form for a recurring architectural problem in a context.

concepts.name: Pattern force
concepts.description: A pressure, constraint, or quality concern that explains why a pattern fits or fails in a situation.

concepts.name: Style mismatch
concepts.description: A poor fit between an architectural style and the system qualities, context, or organization using it.

sections.title: Modeling Architecture Without Drowning in Detail

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 11-12. Supplemental: C4 model notation guidance. This unit focuses on modeling architecture without drowning in detail.

Architecture models select detail intentionally. A useful model hides local implementation details while exposing structure, responsibility, interaction, deployment, information, or operational behavior relevant to a stakeholder question.
The C4 model is one practical way to manage abstraction with system context, container, component, and code levels. The deeper lesson is that models need a purpose, audience, notation, and scope.
Studio: model the same system at context, container, and component levels. Remove any detail that does not answer a stakeholder question at that level.

concepts.name: Architecture model purpose
concepts.description: The stakeholder question or analysis goal that determines what a model should include.

concepts.name: Abstraction level
concepts.description: The degree of detail shown in a model, from broad system context to lower-level implementation structures.

concepts.name: C4 container
concepts.description: A separately deployable or executable unit such as a web app, mobile app, database, or service.

concepts.name: Model notation
concepts.description: The visual or textual convention used to represent architectural elements and relationships.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 11-12. Supplemental: C4 model notation guidance. This unit focuses on architectural interfaces and relationships.

Elements matter because they relate. Interfaces, dependencies, data flows, protocols, ownership lines, and deployment relationships define much of the architecture. A box without its relationships tells only a small part of the story.
Interface detail should match architectural risk. A high-risk integration may need contracts, data semantics, error behavior, versioning, observability, and failure handling described early.
Studio: select one external API integration and document its responsibilities, data contract, failure modes, versioning strategy, and ownership.

concepts.name: Architectural element
concepts.description: A component, service, data store, subsystem, actor, or node that appears in an architecture view.

concepts.name: Architectural relationship
concepts.description: A dependency, interaction, allocation, containment, data flow, or communication link between architectural elements.

concepts.name: Interface contract
concepts.description: The expected behavior, data, errors, protocols, and responsibilities at a boundary between elements.

concepts.name: Relationship semantics
concepts.description: The meaning of a relationship, such as calls, publishes, owns, deploys to, reads from, or depends on.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 16-17. Supplemental: C4 context and container diagrams. This unit focuses on functional viewpoint.

The functional viewpoint describes the system runtime structure in terms of responsibilities and functional elements. It helps stakeholders understand what the system does and how major parts collaborate to deliver behavior.

A functional view should show cohesive responsibilities and meaningful interactions, not every class or method. It is especially useful for dividing work, finding missing behavior, and reasoning about coupling.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 16-17. Supplemental: C4 context and container diagrams. This unit focuses on cohesion, coupling, and functional boundaries.

Boundaries should follow domain meaning, operational ownership, data consistency needs, security requirements, and team structure. A clean-looking diagram can still hide poor boundaries if responsibilities are split unnaturally.

concepts.name: Responsibility leakage
concepts.description: A design problem where behavior crosses boundaries in ways that weaken cohesion or ownership.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 18-19. This unit focuses on information viewpoint.

The information viewpoint focuses on data, information models, ownership, lifecycle, integrity, privacy, and flows. Many architectural failures come from unclear data meaning or inconsistent ownership rather than from code structure alone.
Information modeling at architecture level is not about every database column. It is about the data concepts and flows that shape integration, correctness, compliance, and analytics.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 18-19. This unit focuses on concurrency viewpoint.

The concurrency viewpoint describes independently executing parts of a system and how they coordinate. It exposes processes, threads, tasks, queues, locks, events, scheduling, and synchronization concerns.

Concurrency decisions shape throughput, latency, complexity, failure behavior, and correctness. They should be visible when race conditions, shared state, ordering, back pressure, or parallel work could affect system qualities.
Studio: model an order-processing workflow with queues and workers, then identify one ordering risk and one back-pressure point.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 18-19. This unit focuses on consistency, transactions, and events.

Information and concurrency concerns meet where systems update data over time. Transactions, event streams, eventual consistency, idempotency, and compensating actions all express architectural choices about correctness and coordination.
The architect should decide which operations require strong consistency, which can tolerate delay, and how users and operators will observe or repair inconsistent states.
Studio: pick three operations in an ecommerce system and classify each as strong consistency, eventual consistency, or compensating workflow.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 20-22. Supplemental: arc42 architecture documentation guidance. This unit focuses on development viewpoint.
The development viewpoint describes the static organization of source code, modules, libraries, packages, repositories, build units, dependencies, and development responsibilities.

This view helps teams maintain modifiability. It shows where code should live, how dependencies are controlled, how teams coordinate, and how architectural rules are enforced in the development environment.
Studio: sketch a development view for a service-based application, including repositories, shared libraries, generated clients, and dependency rules.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 20-22. Supplemental: arc42 architecture documentation guidance. This unit focuses on deployment viewpoint.

The deployment viewpoint maps software elements onto infrastructure. It covers nodes, networks, regions, containers, storage, middleware, runtime platforms, availability zones, and environment differences.
Deployment structure affects latency, capacity, resilience, security, cost, observability, and release safety. It is where many abstract qualities become operationally concrete.
Studio: map three containers to cloud infrastructure and identify one latency risk, one availability risk, and one cost driver.

concepts.name: Infrastructure mapping

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 20-22. Supplemental: arc42 architecture documentation guidance. This unit focuses on operational viewpoint.

The operational viewpoint describes how the system is run, monitored, supported, backed up, restored, configured, deployed, and repaired. It turns architecture from a design-time artifact into a live system responsibility.
Operational concerns should influence architecture early. If a system cannot be observed, upgraded, rolled back, scaled, or recovered, its design is incomplete even if its functionality works.
Studio: write an operational readiness checklist for a payment service before production launch.

Controls are architectural and operational mechanisms that reduce risk. They include identity, authorization, encryption, validation, network segmentation, monitoring, audit, least privilege, and secure defaults.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapter 26. Supplemental: SEI tradeoff analysis concepts. This unit focuses on scalability mechanisms.

Scalability is the ability to handle increased load by adding resources, changing allocation, or reducing work. Common mechanisms include caching, partitioning, replication, asynchronous processing, load balancing, and horizontal scaling.

Each mechanism has tradeoffs. Caching can improve latency but create staleness. Partitioning can increase capacity but complicate queries. Replication can improve availability but create consistency challenges.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapter 27. Supplemental: SEI ATAM quality tradeoff framing. This unit focuses on availability, reliability, and failure modes.
Availability is about whether service is usable when needed. Reliability is about correct operation over time. Resilience is about surviving, adapting to, and recovering from failure.

Architects reason about failure modes before they happen. Hardware, networks, dependencies, deployments, data corruption, configuration errors, traffic spikes, and human operations can all cause system failure.
Studio: list five failure modes for a payment checkout path and connect each one to a user-visible consequence.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapter 27. Supplemental: SEI ATAM quality tradeoff framing. This unit focuses on redundancy, recovery, and degradation.

Resilient architectures often use redundancy, health checks, failover, retries, circuit breakers, backups, replication, graceful degradation, and disaster recovery. These tactics must match failure assumptions and business needs.
More redundancy does not automatically mean better architecture. It adds cost, operational complexity, consistency problems, and new failure paths if not designed carefully.
Studio: design a degraded mode for a learning platform when video processing is unavailable but course reading pages still need to work.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapter 27. Supplemental: SEI ATAM quality tradeoff framing. This unit focuses on operational resilience and incident learning.
Resilience depends on operations as much as structure. Observability, alerting, runbooks, drills, ownership, safe deployment, rollback, and incident review all shape the system ability to recover.
Architectural learning should continue after incidents. A post-incident review can reveal missing assumptions, hidden dependencies, poor recovery paths, or decisions that need to be revisited.

modules.title: Week 13: Evolution, Governance, and Architecture Debt

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 28-29. Supplemental: arc42 and SEI documentation guidance. This unit focuses on evolution perspective.

The evolution perspective examines how architecture supports change over time. Systems evolve because of new features, technology changes, regulatory shifts, scale, team growth, incidents, and market learning.

Architectural evolution is not just flexibility. It requires identifying likely change points, isolating volatility, keeping decisions revisable, and preserving enough documentation to make future change safe.
Studio: identify three likely changes for a course platform over two years and design one extension point for each.

concepts.name: Evolution perspective
concepts.description: A perspective focused on how the architecture supports planned and unplanned change over time.

concepts.name: Change driver
concepts.description: A business, technical, regulatory, operational, or user force that may require architecture change.

concepts.name: Volatility point
concepts.description: A part of the system expected to change more often than surrounding elements.

concepts.name: Extension point
concepts.description: A designed place where new behavior or variation can be added with limited disruption.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 28-29. Supplemental: arc42 and SEI documentation guidance. This unit focuses on architecture governance.

Architecture governance is the set of lightweight practices that keeps architecture decisions aligned with goals as work proceeds. It includes decision review, standards, guardrails, documentation expectations, and feedback loops.

Good governance helps teams move faster by clarifying which decisions are local and which require architectural attention. Heavy governance can slow learning and encourage paperwork without improving design.
Studio: define a governance rule for when a team must write an architecture decision record before changing a platform boundary.

concepts.name: Architecture governance
concepts.description: Practices that guide, review, and sustain architectural decisions across delivery work.

concepts.name: Architecture guardrail
concepts.description: A rule, standard, automated check, or review boundary that helps teams make safe local decisions.

concepts.name: Decision authority
concepts.description: The person, team, or forum responsible for approving or owning an architectural decision.

concepts.name: Governance feedback loop
concepts.description: A mechanism that uses delivery experience, incidents, metrics, and reviews to adjust architectural guidance.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 28-29. Supplemental: arc42 and SEI documentation guidance. This unit focuses on architecture debt and refactoring.

Architecture debt appears when current structure makes future work slower, riskier, or more expensive. It can come from shortcuts, outdated assumptions, poor boundaries, inconsistent documentation, or changing business needs.

Architecture refactoring should be tied to business and quality outcomes. The argument is stronger when debt is expressed as risk, delay, incidents, change cost, or lost capability rather than architectural taste.
Studio: write an architecture debt item with impact, evidence, proposed mitigation, cost, and risk of doing nothing.

concepts.name: Architecture debt
concepts.description: A structural or decision-related weakness that increases future cost, risk, delay, or fragility.

concepts.name: Architecture refactoring
concepts.description: A deliberate change to improve architectural structure without primarily adding user-visible features.

concepts.name: Debt evidence
concepts.description: Observed delay, defect, incident, complexity, or cost that demonstrates architectural debt impact.

concepts.name: Migration path
concepts.description: A planned sequence of changes that moves the system from current architecture to a target architecture.

modules.title: Week 14: Evaluation, Communication, and Professional Practice

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 14 and 30. Supplemental: SEI ATAM and Views and Beyond. This unit focuses on architecture evaluation.

Architecture evaluation asks whether the architecture is fit for its intended purpose. Scenario-based methods such as ATAM use stakeholder scenarios to uncover risks, sensitivity points, tradeoffs, and non-risks.
Evaluation does not require perfect certainty. It creates enough shared evidence to improve decisions, reduce unknowns, and make risks explicit before they become expensive.
Studio: run a mini evaluation on one design decision using three scenarios and identify one risk, one tradeoff, and one follow-up experiment.

concepts.name: Architecture evaluation
concepts.description: The assessment of whether an architecture satisfies important concerns, scenarios, constraints, and quality goals.

concepts.name: ATAM
concepts.description: Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method, a structured scenario-based method for analyzing architectural risks and tradeoffs.

concepts.name: Sensitivity point
concepts.description: An architectural decision or parameter where small changes can strongly affect a quality attribute.

concepts.name: Tradeoff point
concepts.description: An architectural decision that affects multiple quality attributes in competing ways.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 14 and 30. Supplemental: SEI ATAM and Views and Beyond. This unit focuses on communicating architecture.

Architecture communication adapts to audience. Executives need risks, options, cost, and business impact. Developers need boundaries, interfaces, decisions, and constraints. Operators need deployment, monitoring, recovery, and ownership.
The architect acts as a translator across concerns. Effective communication uses the smallest set of views and narratives that help stakeholders make better decisions.
Studio: prepare a five-minute architecture briefing for a non-technical sponsor and a separate five-minute briefing for an implementation team.

concepts.name: Architecture narrative
concepts.description: A coherent explanation of the system context, major decisions, tradeoffs, risks, and consequences.

concepts.name: Audience adaptation
concepts.description: Changing architecture communication to match stakeholder knowledge, decisions, and concerns.

concepts.name: Architecture briefing
concepts.description: A concise presentation or walkthrough of architecture information for a particular audience.

concepts.name: Decision framing
concepts.description: Presenting architectural choices in terms of options, consequences, evidence, and stakeholder impact.

content.value: Primary reading: Rozanski and Woods, Chapters 14 and 30. Supplemental: SEI ATAM and Views and Beyond. This unit focuses on capstone architecture package.

The capstone brings the course together. Students define scope, identify stakeholders, write scenarios, choose views, document decisions, apply perspectives, evaluate tradeoffs, and present an architecture package.
A strong final package does not need to be huge. It needs to be coherent, source-backed, stakeholder-aware, explicit about tradeoffs, and honest about risks and assumptions.

Capstone: produce an architecture package for a medium-sized software system with context, functional, information, deployment, operational, two perspectives, five decision records, and an evaluation summary.

concepts.name: Capstone architecture package
concepts.description: A final course artifact combining architecture scope, views, decisions, perspectives, risks, and evaluation evidence.

concepts.name: Architecture coherence
concepts.description: The degree to which views, decisions, rationale, scenarios, and constraints tell a consistent architectural story.

concepts.name: Risk register
concepts.description: A maintained list of architectural risks, impacts, owners, mitigation actions, and status.

concepts.name: Architecture presentation
concepts.description: A structured communication of architecture decisions, tradeoffs, and evidence to stakeholders.
